clue.text: Game F1 driver

blocks.note: first meaning: an old card game for two players
second meaning: Nelson, the Brazilian Formula One world champion of the 1980s

explanation.surface: A racing driver is described as a game, as if the man himself were play.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a racing video game; the two parts are separate meanings, a card game and a Brazilian racing champion's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The card game shares its spelling with the surname of the three-time Formula One world champion Nelson.

clue.text: Pinter play set on top of hill in Cumbria

blocks.note: the playwright Harold's surname, rearranged
first letter of hill

explanation.surface: A Harold Pinter play is staged on a Lake District fell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a noun, a Pinter drama, but it is the instruction to rearrange his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Penrith is a market town in the north of the county, near the Lake District.

clue.text: Living like a bat out of hell?

definitions.text: like a bat out of hell

blocks.note: first meaning: alive, as in the old phrase about judging the living and the dead

blocks.clueFragment: like a bat out of hell
blocks.note: second meaning: very fast

explanation.surface: It asks whether being alive is like a creature fleeing hell.
explanation.walkthrough: The old sense of the word means alive, as in 'the quick and the dead' from the Creed.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective once meant alive and now means fast, and a bat fleeing hell moves at great speed.

clue.text: Stretch or break up in river

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the Exe, a river in Devon
to break is to snap

explanation.surface: Something stretches or breaks while in a river, like an overloaded rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break up' looks like one phrasal verb, but up is a separate instruction in this down clue. The Exe is a river in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide stretch of land, sea or sky, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Encouraging remark made by Hannibal initially in Carthaginian retreat

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the general's first letter is wanted

the single letter goes in the other word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: Punic means relating to Carthage
first letter of the general's name

explanation.surface: Hannibal makes a rousing speech as the Carthaginians fall back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retreat' reads like a military withdrawal, apt for Hannibal, but it reverses the adjective, and the H goes in after the C.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection 'chin up!' is said to cheer someone and keep their spirits from flagging.

clue.text: He made the bloody discovery before Wallbanger

blocks.note: first meaning: William, the physician who showed how blood circulates
second meaning: the word that comes first in the name of a vodka cocktail

explanation.surface: A man found something gory before someone banged on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' looks like a mild British oath or a gory detail; it is literal, about blood. A Harvey Wallbanger is a cocktail of vodka, orange juice and Galliano.
explanation.definitionFit: The English physician William first described the circulation of blood, and his first name begins the cocktail.

clue.text: A physicist and his Nobel work on source of radiation

indicators.note: to work something is to shape and knead it, so these letters are reshaped
the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter
in a down clue one piece on another sits above it, so the rearranged letters come first

blocks.note: these two words rearranged
first letter of radiation

explanation.surface: A physicist's Nobel-winning research concerned where radiation comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Niels Bohr did win a Nobel Prize, in 1922, for work on atomic structure and radiation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish scientist Niels Bohr developed the model of the atom with electrons in fixed orbits.

clue.text: Rara avis in Arizona?

blocks.note: surface reading: a rare bird, Latin for something unusual, spotted in a desert state
setter's reading: the one-of-a-kind mythical bird that rises from its ashes, which is also the name of Arizona's state capital

explanation.walkthrough: Rara avis is Latin for rare bird, used for anything unusual. The legendary firebird was unique, only one alive at a time, and the city shares its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical bird reborn from ashes was unique, a truly rare bird, and gives its name to Arizona's capital city.

clue.text: Film about alien in naval vessel that's out of action

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the creature's short name is read backwards
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: a warship is a naval vessel
ET, the extra-terrestrial of the Spielberg film
a system that is down is not working

explanation.surface: A film about an alien on a naval ship that has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', as in a film about an alien, but here it is the signal to turn the alien round before it boards the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Watership Down is the 1978 animated film of Richard Adams's novel about rabbits.

clue.text: Opposed to sloth around midwinter

indicators.note: mid means the middle, so only the central letters of the season are kept
one piece going around another encloses it

blocks.note: the ai is a three-toed sloth, a crossword favourite
the middle two letters of winter

explanation.surface: Someone is against laziness in the dead of winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The ai is a South American three-toed sloth; it wraps around NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being anti something means being against it, so the preposition matches the phrase.

clue.text: Flexible ape or rigid rodent

blocks.note: these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: It contrasts a bendy ape with a stiff rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a link between two animals, but it is part of the letters to rearrange, and 'flexible' and 'rigid' pull in opposite directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Prairie dogs are burrowing North American ground squirrels, so they belong to the order of gnawing mammals.

clue.text: Contribute by givin' up?

blocks.note: first meaning: to chip in money or effort, as a phrasal verb
second meaning: quitting a habit, written with the dropped g of casual speech

explanation.surface: It asks whether you can contribute by giving something up.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe matters: the answer read as one word with a dropped g is slang for quitting, as in kicking a habit.
explanation.definitionFit: To chip in is to contribute, and kicking a habit, said casually without the final g, means quitting it.

clue.text: Regular issue and good service

blocks.note: even means regular or steady
issue means offspring, such as a son
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A regular magazine issue and good service, like a reliable delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a magazine edition, but it means a child, as in 'died without issue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the Anglican evening prayer service, sung in cathedrals each day.

clue.text: A singer can use the arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things in a new order, as a musician rearranges a tune

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A singer can make use of a musical arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement' fits the musical picture perfectly, but it is the instruction; 'the' supplies three of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A chanteuse is a female singer, especially of popular songs in a nightclub or cabaret.

clue.text: Stage direction sounds bad

blocks.note: noises are sounds
food that has gone off is bad

explanation.surface: An actor complains that a stage direction sounds bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' looks like a verb (it sounds bad) but it is a plural noun. It is also the title of Michael Frayn's farce.
explanation.definitionFit: A script marks sounds made in the wings, unseen by the audience, with this instruction.

clue.text: Use gentle persuasion - providing drinks, by the sound of it

indicators.note: this phrase asks for a word that is said like the clue's word, not spelled like it

blocks.note: Cokes, cans of cola, are drinks

explanation.surface: Persuading someone gently by buying them drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Providing' looks like 'if', but here it just joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To coax someone is to win them over softly with flattery or patience rather than force.

clue.text: What attracts bishop? Getting introduction to actress with sex appeal?

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so just the first letter is kept

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
first letter of actress
'it' is old slang for sex appeal, from the 1927 Clara Bow film

explanation.surface: It asks what draws a bishop: being introduced to an alluring actress.
explanation.walkthrough: The bishop and actress recall the old saucy catchphrase 'as the actress said to the bishop'. IT meaning sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait is anything used to lure fish or prey, so it is literally something that draws them in.

clue.text: Monk getting Russian leader into trouble?

one piece getting into another ends up inside it

blocks.note: bother means trouble
first letter of Russian

explanation.walkthrough: 'Russian leader' suggests a tsar or president, but it just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Monks in a religious order are addressed as Brother, a member of a fraternity.

clue.text: Arctic prison for Spooner's dance

indicators.note: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for muddling his words, means swap the opening sounds of two words

blocks.note: Arctic weather is bitterly cold, and jug is slang for prison; swap the opening sounds of the pair

explanation.surface: An Arctic prison camp holds a dance for Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of BITTER JUG to get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The jitterbug was a fast, acrobatic swing dance popular in America in the 1930s and 1940s.

clue.text: Old photograph of tiny pet, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the words are only one possible order, so they can be rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.walkthrough: Without the usual anagram words, 'perhaps' is the only signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tintype was a Victorian photograph printed directly on a thin iron plate coated with black lacquer.

clue.text: Strait-laced university professor first getting drunk

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a nice contradiction: a strait-laced professor who gets drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uptight is tense and rigidly conventional, much like a person who is prim and prudish.

clue.text: Indian putting hand on knee (not head)

taken as written, before its first letter goes

taken as written

clue.text: Discombobulated acid-head means to join cast

first letter of acid
